body:
aider notices if your repo is dirty, and asks if you want to auto commit the changes. You can suppress this behavior with the `--no-auto-commit` cmd line arg. But this will also stop auto committing the changes that aider itself makes.

The problem you are encountering is that `Coder.get_commit_message()` uses gpt-3.5-turbo to summarize the diffs into a sensible commit message. If the diff is large, it exceeds the 4K context window.

A simple fix would be:

1. Check if the diff is close to or larger than 4 kbytes (4k tokens * 4 bytes/token) and don't even bother sending the messages to gpt. Just return.
2. Catch the `openai.error.InvalidRequestError` and just return.

Maybe print a nice tool_error() message for each of these.

Actually, after typing the above I pasted it into aider and it fixed itself:
https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/commit/32e40a3e1c1d9545c8f92198848a1c91afe67496

body:
I think this is a new issue you're seeing, likely caused by the giant file list as you say.

I just added a check, and aider will only send the file list to gpt if it is less than 100 files. In that case, gpt will only know about the specific files you add to the chat. It won't even know about the existence of other files in the repo, so it won't be able to ask to see any that are relevant.

But ya, if you add the files it needs to the chat then this should work better on large repos.

I am also working on a much more ambitious attempt to manage the limited context window size. But so far it's just some early experiments.

body:
I just pushed changes that allow aider to work with gpt-3.5-turbo. Let me know if it works for you.

GPT-3.5 is not able to reliably generate "edit blocks" to specify changes to files. The best approach is to ask it to simply return a new copy of the entire file, including the changes that it wants to make. Unfortunately, this wastes context window and is a bit slow. But it is fairly reliable.

So you can really only work with smaller source files with 3.5. This is because of the need to read/write the entire file content and the smaller 4 k-token context window.

Aider also disables the "ctags / repo map" feature when using GPT-3.5. That model probably isn't capable of using the additional code context, so it's not worth using up precious context window with the map.

Thanks for trying aider! I'm not sure I fully understand what you are trying to do, but let me offer some suggestions.

The README for aider explains how to enable ctags. You just install the `universal ctags` tool and then run `aider --ctags`. That's all you need to do. It will automatically use ctags to scan **every file** in your git repository.

I gave this a try against the repo you mentioned:

> $ git clone https://github.com/lightningRalf/CrawlGitHub.git  
> $ cd CrawlGitHub  
> $ aider  --ctags  
> Using git repo: .git  

#### > explain the general structure of this project  

The project consists of three files:

1. `.gitignore`: This file is used to specify files and directories that should be ignored by Git when tracking changes in the repository.

2. `fetch_starred_repos.py`: This script fetches the starred repositories of a GitHub user. It contains several variables such as `api_url`, `github_pat`, `headers`, `json_data`, `page`, `response`, `starred_repos`, and `working_directory`. The script likely makes API calls to GitHub to retrieve the starred repositories and stores the information in the `starred_repos` variable.

3. `generate_repo_info.py`: This script generates information about a specific repository. It contains a function `get_readme_url(github_url, default_branch)` and several variables such as `api_url`, `contributors`, `contributors_data`, `contributors_response`, `contributors_url`, `default_branch`, `existing_files`, `existing_numbers`, `forks`, `github_pat`, `headers`, `latest_release`, `markdown_file`, `next_number`, `readme_url`, `releases_data`, `releases_response`, `releases_url`, `repo_data`, `repo_description`, `repo_name`, `response`, `stars`, `urls`, `watching`, and `working_directory`. The script likely makes API calls to GitHub to retrieve various information about the repository, such as contributors, forks, stars, and watchers, and generates a markdown file with this information.

4. `main.py`: This file is not described in the summaries provided. It is likely the main entry point of the project, which calls the functions from the other two scripts to fetch starred repositories and generate repository information.

The general structure of the project is to fetch information about starred repositories and generate detailed information about each repository, possibly for documentation or reporting purposes.

body:
One thing that may not be obvious is that GPT only sees a high level "map" of the repo until you explicitly give it permission to load the content of specific files. The map is built using ctags, and just shows GPT the functions and variables which are defined in each file in the git repo.

But aider doesn't sent GPT the *full content* of any* files, until you explicitly "add them to the chat". You can add files by naming them on the command line or by adding them using `/add` in the chat.

So unless you explicitly add the doc files to the chat, GPT will only see some high level info about them in the repo map.

body:
> I'm continuing to have "is not one of" issues. I asked for a modification for a specific file but the code block wasn't tagged in the parsable format.

Hi @tmm1, I just released version 0.7.0, which has more robust support for GPT-3.5. Aider is now much more permissive at recognizing which files to edit when 3.5 returns malformed instructions (as it often does). I did some benchmarking, and this release of aider performs better at coding editing competency with 3.5 compared to the prior release. Let me know if you have a chance to try it out and if you see improvements.

> I wonder if it makes sense to integrate the new functions api instead, and offer the LLM functions to create and modify files, with json arguments that explicitly include a filename property.

I also roughed in an coding backend for 3.5 which uses the new functions api. Surprisingly it benchmarks significantly worse than the current editing format that relies on markdown backtick fenced codeblocks. I'm going to continue to experiment here, and will hopefully share some quantitative learnings at some point.
author: paul-gauthier

body:
Thanks for the feedback @tomrobinsond. I agree it would be nice for aider to support a larger variety of LLMs.

Other users have used the `--openai-api-base` argument to run aider against other models that can provide an OpenAI-compatible api. This looks like a relevant tool to serve many local models via a compatible api. I haven't tried it myself yet though.

https://github.com/go-skynet/LocalAI

One thing to keep in mind is that it generally requires some model-specific tuning to get prompts and editing formats working well. For example, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 use very different prompts and editing formats in aider right now. So I imagine adopting new LLMs will require a similar effort to tailor the prompting and edit formats.

The latest version of aider includes a major refactor that makes it easy to develop, benchmark and manage a collection of many "coding backends". This should make it easier tailor aider to additional LLMs in the future.
author: paul-gauthier

body:
Hi @paul-gauthier 
Did you look into LocalAI yet? It would be such a great direction to go. We see open-source models such as WizardCoder rocketing in performance. Being able to run locally will allow data-sensitive work to benefit, without as much data-breach risk to contend with (e.g. in medical domains).

body:
Good catch, thanks for reporting. I just pushed a fix. You'll need to install from github to pick it up.

The root of the issue is that GPT-4 won't consistently return properly formatted diffs. The `<<ORIGINAL/>>UPDATED` format aider uses is by far the most reliable format I've discovered. But GPT-4 won't always conform and output even this very simple format.

I've tried asking it to output `diff -c`, `diff -u`, `sed`, and many other formats. GPT-4 does much, much worse on them. Even the new functions api is not looking like a panacea here.

One key issue about the "output format" is that it's easy to "distract" the LLM if you ask it to use too structured or technical of a format. Especially when you're asking it to write code. The coding itself is a challenging task, and asking it to render actual diff or vim or sed editing outputs is going to confuse it. I have absolutely seen the quality of the coding task degrade when the output format is too complex.

Imagine asking a junior developer to "implement this cool feature, but I want you to hand type the diffs required to change the current code".

I'm hoping to write up something more quantitative and concrete about this aspect of AI coding soon.

Thanks for trying aider and reporting this issue and sharing the chat history. That's very helpful information.

It looks to me like this may be a problem with the way aider handles subdirectories on Windows. I will continue to investigate and let you know when I've implemented a solution.

In the meantime, you might want to try and avoid using subdirectories and see if that helps. When starting a new project with aider you could run aider like `aider quorum_scraper.py`. Aider will make a new empty file without suggesting a subdirectory. Then when you ask for code, it will go into that file.

For example, here is the transcript of me doing that and giving aider your initial prompt:

> aider quorum_scraper.py  
>
> Model: gpt-4  
> Creating empty file quorum_scraper.py  
> Files not tracked in .git:  
>   quorum_scraper.py  
> Add them? y  
> Added quorum_scraper.py to the git repo  
> Commit 07b56f3 Added new files to the git repo: quorum_scraper.py  
> Git repo: .git  
> Repo-map: universal-ctags using 1024 tokens  
> Added quorum_scraper.py to the chat.  
> Use /help to see in-chat commands.  

#### I want to make a Quorum web scraper that scrapes text from pages and subpages from http://quorumlanguage.com. The script will create text files so that a large language model can understand them.  

To create a web scraper for the Quorum language website, we will need to use a library like BeautifulSoup to parse the HTML of the website and extract the text. We will also need the requests library to send HTTP requests to the website. 

Here are the steps we will follow:

1. Send a GET request to the main page of the website.
2. Parse the HTML of the main page to find links to subpages.
3. For each subpage, send a GET request to retrieve the HTML.
4. Parse the HTML of each subpage to extract the text.
5. Write the text to a file.

Here's how we can modify your `quorum_scraper.py` file to implement this:

```python
quorum_scraper.py
<<<<<<< ORIGINAL

=======
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import os

def get_page_text(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, 'html.parser')
    return soup.get_text()

def get_subpage_urls(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, 'html.parser')
    return [a['href'] for a in soup.find_all('a', href=True) if a.text]

def write_text_to_file(text, filename):
    with open(filename, 'w') as f:
        f.write(text)

def main():
    url = 'http://quorumlanguage.com'
    subpage_urls = get_subpage_urls(url)
    for i, subpage_url in enumerate(subpage_urls):
        text = get_page_text(subpage_url)
        write_text_to_file(text, f'subpage_{i}.txt')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
>>>>>>> UPDATED
```

This script will create a text file for each subpage on the Quorum language website. The text files will be named `subpage_0.txt`, `subpage_1.txt`, etc.

> Applied edit to quorum_scraper.py  
> Commit 3ea30de aider: Refactor `quorum_scraper.py` to include functions for getting page text, subpage URLs, and writing text to a file, and add a main function that retrieves the subpage URLs, gets the text for each subpage, and writes it to a file.

body:
It's actually quite challenging to convince even GPT-4 to always return properly formatted code edits. As you've noticed, it sometimes just skips a bunch of code with "..." even though the system prompt strongly disallows that. It can make other mistakes sometimes.

If you see that it has returned a bad edit that fails to apply, you can reply and tell it to try again. Saying something like this might help: "your edit block is missing a bunch of code that you replaced with ..., please give me a proper edit that doesn't skip over any code".

Those original/updated sections are called "edit blocks" and you can use that phrase to talk to GPT about mistakes it made with them.

I see that aider reports `Git repo: none` when it starts. Sounds you aren't using a git repo to manage your files? I really recommend it as a way to keep your changes safe, undo mistakes, etc.

Hi @chalsfxx,

I'm sorry to hear you're having trouble setting the OpenAI API key. To address your issue, let's set the environment variable for the API key without using the `set` command. Follow these steps:

1. Press `Win + R` to open the Run dialog.
2. Type `SystemPropertiesAdvanced` and hit `Enter`. This opens the "System Properties" window with the "Advanced" tab selected.
3. At the bottom of the "Advanced" tab, click the "Environment Variables..." button to open the "Environment Variables" window.
4. In the "Environment Variables" window, under the "User variables" section, click the "New..." button.
5. For "Variable name", enter `OPENAI_API_KEY`. For "Variable value", enter your OpenAI API key, then click "OK".
6. Click "OK" to close the "Environment Variables" window, then click "OK" again to close the "System Properties" window.

Now, you should be able to use the OpenAI API with your applications. Keep in mind that you might need to restart any running applications or open new Command Prompt windows for the changes to take effect.

As for your question about GPT-3.5 Turbo and Chatbot API, the API is completely separated out of ChatGPT plus, You need to add billing to your **API** account, you don't need to waste money on ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a product with easy to use UI. But what aider uses is OpenAI API.

Best,

body:
I finally figured this out! It turns out, there is an extension in the Oobabooga webui called  "openai" that appeared to be the thing that needed enabling.

For future people trying to get this to work try the following steps:

1. Open oobabooga-text-generation-webui
2. Under the "Session" tab (or "Interface" on older versions)
3. Check the box under extensions labeled "openai". This will enable the openai compatible api. You do not need to disable the other API extension.
4. Apply and restart the UI
5. Call aider with `aider --openai-api-base http://localhost:5001/v1 --openai-api-key dummy`

If you followed all those steps, you should be able to easily use the webui with Aider.

body:
Thanks for trying aider and for your interest in experimenting with the repo map.

Here is the code that determines whether to use a repo map:

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/166ecdcbd0b86847088dc195ede37f7b77227859/aider/coders/base_coder.py#L167

So to enable it for gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, you could add a `self.use_repo_map=True` here, so that it is enabled on the model:

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/166ecdcbd0b86847088dc195ede37f7b77227859/aider/models.py#L58

You also need update the prompts used by the wholefile coder. To use a repo-map, it will need a `repo_content_prefix`:

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/166ecdcbd0b86847088dc195ede37f7b77227859/aider/coders/wholefile_prompts.py#L42

You can consult the editblock coder for an example of the `repo_content_prefix`. But you probably also need to introduce the concepts of "read-only" and "read-write" files in the other prompts, similar to the editblock coder.

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/166ecdcbd0b86847088dc195ede37f7b77227859/aider/coders/editblock_prompts.py#L53

I worry that GPT-3.5 won't be able to understand that the repo map is read-only content. It will probably try and "edit" the repo-map files.

I plan to eventually explore this, but I am not optimistic based on my prior experience with prompting 3.5 for code editing.

body:
When you launch aider from the command line, does it report `Repo-map: universal-ctags using 1024 tokens` ? That will let you know for sure that aider is able to find and use your universal ctags installation.

Also, aider tries to "distill" down the full ctags data in order to fit the repo-map into a specified token budget (1024 tokens by default). Otherwise large repos would have maps that would just exhaust the context window. This is functionality from the Future Work section of the repo map article, but it's live in the tool now. I just haven't had a chance to write it up.

If you do `RepoMap(map_tokens = 1024*1024)` to tell it to use an extremely large number of tokens, it should include everything that ctags outputs.

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/166ecdcbd0b86847088dc195ede37f7b77227859/aider/repomap.py#L72

* @param {string} libraryName - Name of the library.
* @param {Object} summaryData - Summarized documentation data.
*/
function saveSummary(libraryName, summaryData) {
 const outputPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'summaries', `${libraryName}.json`); // Adjust directory structure as needed
 fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, JSON.stringify(summaryData, null, 2));
 console.log(`Saved summary for ${libraryName} to ${outputPath}`);
}

/**
* Saves the detailed documentation index to a specified directory.
*
* @param {string} libraryName - Name of the library.
* @param {Object} indexData - Detailed documentation data.
*/
function saveIndex(libraryName, indexData) {
 const outputPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'indexes', `${libraryName}.json`); // Adjust directory structure as needed
 fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, JSON.stringify(indexData, null, 2));
 console.log(`Saved index for ${libraryName} to ${outputPath}`);
}
```

body:
Thanks for trying aider and making these suggestions!

The headline of the commit message is generated by gpt-3.5 as a sensible summary of the changes. You can see the prompt here:

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/fb5af6ec8bb70b2ca4d633d6ec890b94c505d9c0/aider/prompts.py#L5

The remaining body of the commit message just serves as a record of the chat conversation which resulted in the commit, code blocks and all.

The code blocks generated by GPT are not *exactly* the same as the diffs which are applied to the files. Because GPT is often sloppy/imprecise in its code editing, aider has to take liberties and use "best efforts" to apply the suggested edit to the files.

So there is some value in having a record of "what GPT said to do" in addition to the actual git diffs.
author: paul-gauthier

body:
Thanks for clarifying!
I suggest keeping a record of conversations under `.aider/conversations-record/` - it will be tracked by git by default, however the user may opt out by `.gitignore`ing it.
Thus we conform to the usual use of git commit messages - tracking intentions, change summaries and similar.

If `.aider/conversations-record/` is commited together with the relevant changes, then you can see a similar git log like this:
```shell
git log --patch
```
or
```shell
git log -p
```

body:
Thanks for trying Aider!

Aider reads JSON from Universal Ctags but does not send JSON to GPT. It sends an efficient hierarchical tree format. 

You can find more details in this write-up about the repo map:

https://aider.chat/docs/ctags.html
author: paul-gauthier

body:
Thanks for trying aider! 

By default, aider only uses 1024 tokens worth of the context window for the repository map. You can try increasing that by using the `--map-tokens` command line switch. 

That might help when you are working with a very large repository.

I am still tuning a few ideas.
1.  What I tried to describe above: Have GPT4 place cursors in the code to make edits. The idea here would be chatGPT regurgitating a few tokens one by one and placing a Pipe as cursor in it while doing so. I could then find the matching tokens in the code and place a "cursor" accordingly. It is quite similiar to your approach, only responding more token efficient for the part to be replaced. I also hope this would lead it to make smaller edits.
> Place two cursors before at the beginning and end of the snippet. Use '|' to represent a cursor. For both cursors, return sections that include the cursor and the 10 characters immediately before and after it, to give context for positioning.

2. if there is a bash way to do edits, explaining the concept would be easy. I asked chatgpt and it suggested `sed`. It does howevery not support multiline edits so I tried this:
> To make an edit answer with:
> - a regex selecting a part of code that will be removed, keep it short
> - [optional] new code to insert at the position

Both approaches gave decent results on a few experiments in the playground, but I  guess they would still be prone to errors.

body:
The best part of aider is that it isn't tied to any specific editor or IDE.  The terminal is universal, it's much faster, easier to develop for, you don't need to use a mouse, etc.  While I do think making it easier to manage context (which files are included, etc) would be very worthwhile and is probably the number one thing that would improve aider (hard to improve on excellent! it's a good thing), I don't think it's worthwhile to compromise aider's core design principles to do so.  Specifically the design principles of being editor agnostic and a completely text-based interface.

If someone made a very simple VS code plugin that simply sent aider commands like "add file my_file.py to context", "paste selection into aider", "add open tabs to aider context", etc, that should fulfill most of the asks AND require little to no maintenance.  By "send aider commands" I mean literally clicking a button (or keyboard shortcut) will send a text string into the VS code terminal followed by a newline.  If you start adding GUIs and advanced functionality you end up with another POC that is abandoned after a few months, that's just how things go.

body:
Have done a bit more of a deep dive into fleet context and am thinking about the following approach

- use @ prefix in query (like cursor) to tell aider which libraries we want to get context from (e.g. @langchain @openai @pandas etc.)
- use the [fleet langchain integration](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/fleet_context) to get the documents that are relevant to that query 
- add them as context to the query

@paul-gauthier how would you feel about adding a langchain dependency to the project?

We could also have it so that the document retrieval is a separate query `@langchain how to use fleet-context to retrieve embeddings` with the outcome being only some documents added to our context window. Or it could be 'achieve goal xyz @pandas @langchain' where the document retrieval is done in the same step as directing Aider. Keen to hear people's thoughts on which approach they would prefer?

In terms of options I think we could
a) give the user a lot of visibility / control over the context retrieved (think parallel to how files are currently tracked). /list-contexts /clear-contexts /rm-context 3 etc.
b) give them less control - contexts are more or less invisible in the ui
c) maybe b) by default with an option to jump into a) for people who like complexity & control?

Given the overall strategy of wanting people to think less about the context and just have aider figure it out maybe we can think about the context management commands more as internal functions that aider will start to call as it gets more capable and keep the ui focused on what the user wants to achieve?

In terms of integrating with fleet, I notice the author mentioning the intention to add rust and js in the future as well as moving beyond the openai embedding model to some open ones. I think the main call we'd need to make is do we leverage the fleet api for querying contexts or try and query them locally

Yes, the goal is to eventually have aider/GPT manage all of the file access automatically! But we aren't there yet. This is ongoing work. You can see some discussion about next steps in the [future work](https://aider.chat/docs/ctags.html#future-work) section of the repo-map documentation.

In many cases, the current ctags repo-map enables the kind of request you're describing. GPT can figure out which files it will need to edit and ask permission to open them. But the current repo-map is not always enough, depending on the complexity of the repo, etc.

The repo-map has another important function. Even if GPT is only editing code inside one file, it needs to understand the overall structure of the codebase and be aware of other subsystems, modules, etc. The code it is writing may need to call other modules, etc. The repo-map provides this context as well. So even if you only add 1-2 files to the chat, GPT will have the big picture in hand when it edits them.

body:
There's two other major things we can do to alleviate the context pressure:

## Solution 1: Summarization

If our context grows beyond the limit, we can apply summarization techniques to reduce the input so that it fits in the context window. This can even be done with a custom prompt so that the summarization is done with the semantics of the original request in mind. For example, we can prompt: "reduce this text by 75%. do so by first eliminating any content that is not relevant to <user's aider query>".

This summarization prompt is applied by mapping the prompt onto a set of chunks, or a rolling window, or a divide & conquer algorithm.

## Solution 2: Embeddings Search in Vector DB

In this solution, we take the entire codebase, divide the entire thing up into chunks, generate embeddings, then store those in a vector db (chroma db). We can then generate embeddings on the user's query at runtime and search the vector db for vectors closest in proximity to the input, which will be semantically similar to the input. This vector search can give us just the small chunks of relevant info that we can put in the context window.

body:
In a project with very large (perhaps legacy) code files, I'm finding that even /add'ing one very large file in Aider can add to time/costs significantly. I'm using local models, so I'm more concerned about time, but cost in terms of tokens is correlated.

I would much prefer if Aider could allow the LLM to read _subsets_ of a file, rather than the entirety of the file, especially during the planning phase (e.g. /ask or architect mode). If the LLM determines a file needs to be completely added to apply the fix or feature successfully so be it, but right now even planning uses a massive amount of tokens because the entirety of every file of potential interest is added to the context.

The only partial workaround I'm aware of, is for me to manually manage the context with /read and /add, which means I pretty much need to pre-architect the solution, and even then there's no way for me to tell it to only look at subsets of those files that are actually relevant.

By comparison, a human software engineer would only read the most likely portions of the potentially relevant files before applying a fix or building a feature, they would not read all potentially relevant files from top to bottom.

The result of this is that for use with a local model, the inefficient use of context with regard to relevant code snippets makes it not very useful except for very narrow uses where I want it to do something trivial to a small file.

To be clear, the local models I'm using have large context (100k-200k), such as GLM 5.2 Q5. I'm not talking about small or more limited models. But they slow down significantly with unnecessary context usage.

body:
Thanks for trying aider and it's great to hear you've been able to get 8K lines of code out of it already! And thanks for providing such a clear and detailed issue describing the problem you're having.

GPT-3.5 is quite unreliable, and often disobeys the system prompt instructions. When that happens, you get results like what you've shown in your "not working" screencast. Even worse, if you "tweak" the system prompt to try and make things work better for one codebase, you may end up making it worse for (many) other codebases.

I spend a lot of effort trying to make GPT-3.5 produce good output and make sure I don't introduce regressions with new releases of aider. As part of that, I've developed a fairly extensive [benchmarking suite](https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html). It uses aider to try and solve 133 coding exercises, and keeps track of how many of them pass all unit tests. This lets me objectively compare whether new version of aider are better or worse at coding than old versions.

I checked cdf8f9a and the latest build, and both of them perform pretty much identically on the benchmark. I have also reviewed all the relevant code changes between cdf8f9a and latest, and nothing jumps out at me as a likely cause for a regression.

This probably means that you're just having bad luck with GPT-3.5. It will also tend to do worse as the size of the codebase increases. Some suggestions that might help you:

  - When you `/add` files, be selective. Only add the files that GPT needs to see to accomplish the task you're going to give it. This might help GPT-3.5 focus and follow instructions. It also saves you money in token costs.
  - If you have access to GPT-4, use it instead. It is much more reliable.

I will keep looking into this, but I wanted to get back you with my research so far.

The https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/commit/de02038a7e25f4edeb3d2992a53be6debd193664 commit makes a innocuous change to the `/token` command that prints a report of context window token usage. It is unrelated to the way aider communicates with GPT related to code changes.

But that commit is on a branch for PR #58 which rationalized the support for unicode encodings. So it's possible your bisect is just telling us that something in that PR is causing a problem. Your screencasts above seem to be from a Mac, which handles files as utf-8 by default. The PR was mainly to help Windows users, because Windows doesn't default to utf-8.

Any chance some of your files have non-utf8 encodings?

Another thing you could try is run `aider --verbose`. This will show you everything (!) that aider is sending to GPT. You could run it that way on https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/commit/cdf8f9a4b2b4a65993227ac5af1eaf3f1b85c9d8 and on the latest and inspect the output to look for differences.

```
aider gitlab_epic_analyzer/* README.md pyproject.toml .env \
    --verbose \
    --msg "add a function get_projects in GitlabAPI that finds all projects in a group and its subgroups" \
    > verbose-output.txt

body:
Thanks for trying aider, and sorry you ran into this issue. And thank you for such an excellent bug report including a sample repo to reproduce the bug!

I just made a PR that attempts to fix the root cause, which is that `git ls-files` mangles unicode filenames by default and escapes them:

```
$ git ls-files
README.md
"doc/f\303\244nny_dirname/README.md"
"doc/system\303\274berblick.md"
```

There is a git config setting to disable this behavior. Aider now invokes `git -c core.quotepath=off ls-files` to get unmangled filenames:

```
$ git -c core.quotepath=off ls-files
README.md
doc/fänny_dirname/README.md
doc/systemüberblick.md
```

body:
Thanks for very nice comments about aider and for reporting this issue.

The latest release (v0.8.3) assumes that you want all the files you work on with aider to be part of git. This is mainly to ensure the safety of your files' contents. GPT can sometimes make (huge) mistakes when you ask it to edit a file, to the point of deleting most of a file's content, etc. This isn't super common, but it happens. Making sure the files are in git means it's always easy to undo a GPT mistake (big or small).

If you prefer to operate without using git, you can run aider with `--no-git`.

I am curious to get your thoughts about this change. I don't want aider to use git by default if that causes some problem for people that I didn't anticipate.

As you noted, the root cause was inconsistent handling of paths when aider is launched from a directory which is not the the git working directory (root). I made things consistent.

author: alexanderkjeldaas

body:
Ah I see. In my experience coding with GPT, in this situation I would simply make an edit in my editor to fix/improve the code, commit that and move on (kind of like your option 2). That fixes the **code**, but doesn't worry about the fact that there's a commit in the history which wasn't perfect.

I'm not sure it's in scope for aider to strive for a perfect commit history. Coding with GPT is very much a collaborative and iterative process. Aider relies on git for safety so that you can always undo something that GPT does.

 If you want to tidy up the commit history, you probably need to use git on the command line to rebase or `--amend`, etc.

author: MohHeader

body:
> Have you considered postpone the point when aider ask to commit dirty change. For example, aider can determine whether it needs to make change after GPT replies; we can ask the user to commit dirty change at that point.

Yes, I've been thinking about this quite a bit since you opened this issue, and I agree it would be desirable to minimize the number of times that we need to commit the dirty repo. 

But unfortunately, I don't think there's an easy way to make that better. 

Whenever you send a message to GPT, aider sends along the full content of all the files which have been added to the chat, as well as a bunch of data about the functions and variables in many other files in the repository. This other data is called the repository map. 

GPT is then free to reply with edits to any of the files that are in the chat session, but those edits may depend on data in the repository map. So it seems prudent to make sure that we have a clean repository before each message is sent to GPT. That way we can safely apply its edits to a known state and make it easy to undo back to that state if needed.

body:
Thanks for trying aider and reporting this issue. You seem to have 2 issues going on here:

#### Aider is scanning all of your `node_modules` directory.

Aider scans all the files in your git repo once, and then re-scans any files which are modified. 

Have you added `node_modules` and all of its content to your git repo? Normally folks do not do that. If it is in your repo, that would explain why aider trying to scan all of those files.

#### Aider is encountering lots of non-utf8 files.

Aider prints a warning message if it encounters a file which does not match the encoding it is using.  The warnings are harmless as long as those files aren't important to the work you want to do with GPT. Aider will remember that the file can't be decoded and ignore it. 

Or, if all your files are in a non-utf8 encoding, you can specify it with the `--encoding` command line switch.

body:
I don't know how this happened but I fixed it and it works fine
I'm glad I can now try it and explore it

For those facing such a problem, do the following

Update Pipe to the latest version:
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

In the process of installing Adar, use this line 
py -m pip install aider-chat

instead of:
pip install aider-chat


To run it you can use this command
python -m aider.main --model  gemini/gemini-1.5-pro-latest --browser


You can only change the model as you wish by changing its name and do not forget to add the API for module 

as ex
export OPENAI_API_KEY=<key> # Mac/Linux
setx   OPENAI_API_KEY <key> # Windows
export GEMINI_API_KEY=<key> # Mac/Linux
setx   GEMINI_API_KEY <key> # Windows

It was really tiring and stressful. It took me two days to try to run it, but it wouldn't work, but I'm glad I discovered and learned a lot of things.


use py -m  before aider because 
ex: py -m aider --model gemini/gemini-1.5-pro-latest --browser


When you use the py -m aider command, Python's module system takes care of locating and running the aider module. This works because Python knows where to find its installed modules and packages.


Why the Other Command Does Not Work

aider --model gemini/gemini-1.5-pro-latest --browser
When you run this command directly, the shell (command prompt) needs to know where to find the aider executable. The error message:


'aider' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file.
indicates that aider is not in your system's PATH. The PATH is an environment variable that tells the operating system where to look for executables.

Solutions
Ensure aider is Installed Globally: If aider is a Python script or module, make sure it's installed in the global Python environment and that the Python environment's scripts directory is in your PATH.

Use the Python Launcher: Continue using py -m aider, which ensures that Python manages the module lookup and execution.

Modify PATH: Add the directory containing the aider executable to your PATH environment variable. This allows the command prompt to locate aider when you run it directly.

body:
It's not exactly what you're looking for but you can get close to your desired behavior by running aider with the `--no-auto-commit` flag and then just run `/commit` and it will just use a short gpt3.5 generated commit message without the big diff.

The main thing to watch out for is if you run a bunch of edits without committing and the last one makes a mess of things you could lose any edits you have made since your last commit.

Re the costs, you might want to run the `/tokens` command periodically to make sure you are aware of how many tokens are being sent down and reset your chat history and drop files that aren't needed. I found my costs went down a lot when I started paying attention to the token count.

I also found it useful to use 3.5 for simple tasks like starting new files or writing a first draft of code and gpt4 for edits and enhancements - saves costs and can also save time (when it works), but runs the risk of having to do a bunch of rework if the task was too hard for 3.5

body:
Thanks for trying aider and reporting this issue.

I think the root cause is that you're asking too much from GPT-3.5. Asking it to create a multi-file application with a bunch of specific details all in one go is going to be too much for it.

The [tips section on the homepage](https://aider.chat/#tips) recommends: *Large changes are best performed as a sequence of thoughtful bite sized steps, where you plan out the approach and overall design. Walk GPT through changes like you might with a junior dev. Ask for a refactor to prepare, then ask for the actual change. Spend the time to ask for code quality/structure improvements.*

That sort of step-by-step coding is critical for GPT-3.5.

If you have access to GPT-4, I think you would have much better results.

body:
Thanks for trying aider and reporting this issue.

It looks like you pasted a wall of code into the chat prompt, and in your environment each line was sent to aider separately. So aider sent GPT a message (including system prompts, context, chat history, etc) for every line you pasted. In some environments a multi-line paste will be delivered to aider as a single input. It depends on your OS/terminal/settings.

As @MohHeader said, to do multi-line messages you should start them with `{` on a blank line and end with `}` on another blank line. This will deliver them to aider as a single input, and have them sent to GPT as a single message.
author: paul-gauthier

body:
One complication is that aider intercepts ^C so that you can use it to interrupt GPT. In the version you were using, you need to ^C twice during the same "message" to actually interrupt and exit the program. This wasn't happening for you, because you were inside a tight loop of sending each pasted line to GPT. So each ^C was happening within a different "message".

I just updated aider so that if there are 2 keyboard interrupts within 2 seconds it will exit. This would have made it easier for you to stop aider after pasting in the giant list of lines/messages.

This is available in the main branch. You can get it by installing the latest version from github:

```
python -m pip install git+https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider.git
```

If you have a chance to try it, let me know if it works better for you.

body:
Thanks for providing those logs. That helped me reproduce the problem. It's related to issue #95.

The root cause was inconsistent handling of paths when aider is launched from a directory which is not the the git working directory (root). I made things consistent.

Now, when you are using in-chat commands insider aider you are always working with paths that are relative to the git working directory, even if you launch aider from elsewhere in your filesystem (inside or outside of the git repo). I think this the simplest and clearest way to handle things. It's worth noting that it handles the case where you run `aider /path/to/a/git/repo` from a place completely outside that repo. That was the situation in your logs above.

Thanks again for the help debugging this.

body:
Funnily enough, aider provided an example implementation:

---

> /help how do I restore previously added files as well?

To restore previously added files along with the chat history when restarting aider, you can use the
--restore-chat-history flag in combination with the --file option. Here's how you can do it:

 1 First, exit your current aider session if you haven't already.
 2 When restarting aider, use both the --restore-chat-history flag and the --file option with a wildcard to
   include all previously added files. For example:

    aider --restore-chat-history --file "*" --model bedrock/anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0

   The --file "*" option will attempt to add all files that were previously part of the chat session.
 3 If you know specific files or directories you want to include, you can list them explicitly:

    aider --restore-chat-history --file file1.py file2.java src/* --model
    bedrock/anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0


This approach will restore both your chat history and the files that were part of your previous session.

Keep in mind that the --file option with wildcards might add more files than were originally in your chat,
so you may need to use the /drop command to remove any extra files that were unintentionally added.

If you frequently work with the same set of files, you might consider creating a shell script or alias that
includes both the --restore-chat-history flag and the --file options with your commonly used files.

Remember, you can always use the /add and /drop commands within the aider chat to fine-tune which files are
included in your session after starting up.

I've done some experimenting and gotten aider to work against the openrouter api - https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/compare/main...joshuavial:aider:openrouter-hacks has some quick and dirty changes that let me mess around

Main noticings are
- llama 2 wasn't working, would break after generating a few lines
- google palm 2 codechat generated nice code, but really didn't listen to directions about file format that much, my gut feel is it will need a custom coder, but could perform well against it. No streaming so it felt slower, even though it was pretty quick
- claude v2 could create diffs fairly reliably and had good speed, I didn't test the full 100k context but overall I got useful code out of it without too much wrangling. 
- claude v1 was very fast, but felt more fragile than gpt-3.5 - might be good for analyzing a large code base
- both claudes are whiny and would sometimes get into a "I can't ethically create code without more permission / context" particularly the v1. I was just making cli games so it felt like they are a bit oversensitive on the safety front.

I didn't mess with the gpt-4-32k context but it would be pretty easy to test.

I've seen comments in the openrouter discord about rate limits being proportional to the amount of credits you buy, it's a work in progress though but at the moment rate limits are unclear.  It also sounds like they are throttled on the amount of gpt-4-32k access they get so I would expect that to be a bit patchy.

But overall results felt promising and I think it would be a good feature to implement.

If you want to play around then you can use the code above as a starting point (still needs a bunch of work to make it robust) and then you can set your openai api key and base and use commands like `aider --model google/palm-2-codechat-bison --edit-format whole` and ` aider --model anthropic/claude-2 --edit-format diff` to see how the different models perform.

Per the FAQ and info above in the issue, there are already some useful hooks for connecting to other LLMs. A number of users have been using them to experiment with local LLMs. Most reports haven't been very enthusiastic about how they perform with aider compared to GPT-3.5/4.

Aider does have a [modular system for building different "coder" backends](https://aider.chat/docs/faq.html#can-i-change-the-system-prompts-that-aider-uses), allowing customization of prompts and edit formats.

So all the raw materials seem to be available to get aider working with specific new models. I'm always happy to advise as best I can. And if you see evidence that a particular model has the potential to work well with aider, that would exciting news.

When it comes to the coding capabilities of local LLMs, I believe that the HumanEval (pass@1) is the most important metric.

The [leaderboard](https://llm-leaderboard.streamlit.app/) lists "Starcoder-16b" as the best open model with a score of 0.336 compared to GPT-4 score of 0.67.

I don't have a machine powerful enough to run it but I think that with minor tweaking it should perform as well as GPT-3.5

All this being said, I'm not a dev and I haven't tested any of this and honestly don't fully understand all the steps that autonomous agents like Aider take to get it to work.

@ystoll ahhh I see.

I load the model through the command-line at start:

```
OPENEDAI_DEBUG=True server.py \
    --model-dir /path/to/my/models \
    --loader exllamav2_hf \
    --model CodeLlama-34B-instruct-4.0bpw-h6-exl2 \
    --max_seq_len 16384 \
    --listen \
    --api \
    --extensions openai \
    --mlock \
    --settings codellama-34b-settings.yaml \
    --verbose
```

Then here is `codellama-34b-settings.yaml`:

```
max_new_tokens: 16384
max_new_tokens_min: 1
max_new_tokens_max: 16384
truncation_length: 16384
truncation_length_min: 0
truncation_length_max: 16384
auto_max_new_tokens: false
max_tokens_second: 0
ban_eos_token: false
add_bos_token: false
skip_special_tokens: false
stream: true
instruction_template: codellama-34b
rope_freq_base: 1000000
temperature: 0.01
top_p: 0.5
top_k: 20
typical_p: 0.0
num_beams: 5
```

And `instruction-templates/codellama-34b.yaml` (requires [my patch](https://github.com/oobabooga/text-generation-webui/pull/3918) to work):
```
user: ""
bot: ""
turn_template: "<|user|><|user-message|>\n[/INST]\n<|bot|><|bot-message|>\n[INST]\n"
context: "[INST]\n<<SYS>>\n<|system-message|>\n<</SYS>>\n\n"
system_message_default: "Answer the questions."
```

Adjust to your situation, obviously. I have not had the context window error issue anymore since setting this up, but obviously I have not yet been able to run the benchmark, so...

EDIT: Note: I've been messing with prompts all day, so be sure to set the eos/bos settings and template and tokenizer_config.json in the model correctly for your situation!

EDIT#2: I've used this template for wizardcoder-34b:
```
user: ""
bot: ""
turn_template: "<|user|><|user-message|>\n\n### Response:<|bot|><|bot-message|>\n\n"
context: "<|system-message|>\n\n### Instruction:\n"
system_message_default: "Answer the questions."
```

And these two with spicyboros-c34b-2.2 (it supports two different prompts, so I tested them both):
```
user: ""
bot: ""
turn_template: "<|user|><|user-message|>\nENDINSTRUCTION\n<|bot|><|bot-message|>\nBEGININSTRUCTION\n"
context: "BEGININPUT\n<|system-message|>\nENDINPUT\n\nBEGININSTRUCTION\n"
system_message_default: "Answer the questions."
```
```
user: ""
bot: ""
turn_template: "<|user|><|user-message|>\nASSISTANT:<|bot|><|bot-message|>\nUSER:"
context: "<|system-message|>\nUSER:"
system_message_default: "Answer the questions."
```

body:
[Deepseek Coder 33B](https://huggingface.co/TheBloke/deepseek-coder-33B-instruct-GGUF) providing me with the best local results so far. The 6.7B was useless.

Using `llama.cpp` (latest git version is wise, I used [b1492](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b1492) but there are newer releases already):

Llama server (localhost:8080):
```./server -t 16 -m deepseek-coder-33b-instruct.Q4_K_S.gguf -c 6120 --timeout 30 -ngl 65```
I actually used a 6120 context size rather than 16384 due to VRAM limitations, but up to 16384 should work. Using 16 threads because I have a 16 core, reduce to your setup, not sure those are really relevant as I'm offloading the entire model to the GPU here.

Llama to OpenAI proxy server (from `examples/server` subdirectory of your llama.cpp install) (localhost:8081)
```python api_like_OAI.py --chat-prompt "You are an AI programming assistant, utilizing the Deepseek Coder model, developed by Deepseek Company, and you only answer questions related to computer science. For politically sensitive questions, security and privacy issues, and other non-computer science questions, you will refuse to answer.\n" --user-name "\n### Instruction:\n" --ai-name "\n### Response:\n" --system-name "\n"```

Aider benchmark (in docker so not using localhost):
`OPENAI_API_BASE=http://172.17.0.1:8081/v1 OPENAI_KEY=dummy python3.10 benchmark/benchmark.py "$NAME_BENCHMARK" --new --clean --threads 1 --edit-format whole --verbose`

```
test-cases: 134
model: gpt-3.5-turbo
edit_format: whole
commit_hash: 93184d1
num_error_outputs: 1
num_user_asks: 1
num_exhausted_context_windows 0
test_timeouts: 4

43.3% correct after try 0
52.2% correct after try 1

duration: 31.8 sec/test-case
```

Tests run on an RTX4090. No tweaking done to either the model or Aider, these are "out-of-the-box" results. In theory this is competitive with gpt-3.5-turbo.

I have moved away from `text-generation-webui` (aka `oobabooga`) and `llama-cpp-python[server]` due to them being perpetually out of date for the latest models due to embedding specific `llama.cpp` versions, and ultimately nothing but trouble for this usecase. Way easier to just use the real `llama.cpp`.

body:
> I agree, i get much better results with Claude 3, than you for your great work @paul-gauthier

My initial findings show that its capabilities are at least comparable to those of GPT-4, with a similar level of correct code outputs. It also seems to have a lower tendency towards the 'lazy' factor and produces responses that nearly reach the maximum token limit. I believe that even if it is marginally less capable than GPT-4 overall, its enhanced attention mechanism, which covers all 200,000 tokens in the context window, could significantly outperform GPT-4's 128,000-token cross-attention mechanism when dealing with large code bases. The latter often creates hallucinations in context due to its less reliable recall.

Although I don't utilize Aider, I recognize its importance as a data source, and Paul's benchmarks have been illuminating regarding its real-world performance. For a project like Aider, the Claude 3 series of models could represent a substantial improvement, particularly in response formatting and having a much better context memory of the entire codebase. This advancement could be a significant step forward until, presumably, GPT-5 surpasses it with an even better attention mechanism for its context window.

body:
@krrishdholakia Alas, it seems that running `aider` with `--model "gpt-3.5-turbo` fails to properly generate a working repomap for Claude to reference. Fortunately, I've come up with a better workaround (at least until Claude is officially supported).

After installing `aider` with `pip`, navigate to the directory in which it was installed, and edit the `openai_aliases` dictionary on line 108 of `../site-packages/aider/models/openai.py` like so:

# Before:

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/3ab49f1df351d947d76d5e333326f9fd416e5f20/aider/models/openai.py#L108-L116

# After:

```python
openai_aliases = {
    # claude-3-opus
    "anthropic/claude-3-opus-20240229": "gpt-4-vision-preview",
    # gpt-3.5
    "gpt-3.5-turbo": "gpt-3.5-turbo-0613",
    "gpt-3.5-turbo-16k": "gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613",
    # gpt-4
    "gpt-4-turbo-preview": "gpt-4-0125-preview",
    "gpt-4": "gpt-4-0613",
    "gpt-4-32k": "gpt-4-32k-0613",
}
```

After adding the above dictionary entry for Claude, you should be able to run the following without issue:

`aider --openai-api-base "http://0.0.0.0:4000" --model "anthropic/claude-3-opus-20240229"`

Not only will this result in a properly generated repomap, but it will also set sane defaults with regard to context size (i.e., ~100,000 tokens) and edit format (i.e., diff edit blocks). I haven't tested whether images work like they do with `gpt-4-vision-preview`, but in theory, if `litellm` can handle the API translation, I think they might!

body:
I think a bunch of this is already supported? Aider has `Model` and `Coder` objects. I think they only need to be gently extended to support the vision you are describing.

The Model is providing defaults for which coder backend to use, context window size, whether a repo map should be used and a couple of other details. It also attempts to validate sane model names (currently only from the OpenAI naming scheme).

The Coders implement different code editing prompts and backends.

You can choose the Model with `--model` and you can override the default editing backend with `--edit-format` to select any of the Coders. There's some support for overriding other defaults of a given Model, and I was expecting to add switches for that.

The concept of a Transport sounds interesting. I am a bit concerned about trying to support a large number of different APIs/wrappers/abstractions that all lead to the same bag of models. But I haven't thought deeply about this yet.

Thanks for logging the issue, I'm not too familiar with Jupyter notebooks but these approaches might be useful

* you can use the --no-auto-commits flag which would give you complete control over your git flow.
* I find gpt-4 is quite aggressive in how much wrapping content it creates when generating a diff. Adding instructions like "please make the diff as small as possible" can correct this behaviour - though it might also make it a bit more fragile
* you could try writing the prompt in the cell as markdown and then instructing it to follow that instructions above the cell marked as TODO - I've been experimenting with putting instructions in the code as comments which means I don't have to think as much about the prompt I type into aider.

body:
The eventual goal is for aider/GPT to figure out all of this by itself, but it is a work in progress. See the comment below, which I've copied from issue #74 for some additional information.

https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/issues/74#issuecomment-1631601492

Yes, the goal is to eventually have aider/GPT manage all of the file access automatically! But we aren't there yet. This is ongoing work. You can see some discussion about next steps in the [future work](https://aider.chat/docs/ctags.html#future-work) section of the repo-map documentation.

In many cases, the current ctags repo-map enables the kind of request you're describing. GPT can figure out which files it will need to edit and ask permission to open them. But the current repo-map is not always enough, depending on the complexity of the repo, etc.

The repo-map has another important function. Even if GPT is only editing code inside one file, it needs to understand the overall structure of the codebase and be aware of other subsystems, modules, etc. The code it is writing may need to call other modules, etc. The repo-map provides this context as well. So even if you only add 1-2 files to the chat, GPT will have the big picture in hand when it edits them.
author: paul-gauthier

body:
Aider sends the most useful *subset* of the full repo map to GPT, based on analysis of the entire codebase. If you are asking about a minor function, that may not be in the default repo map.

You can see the actual condensed repo map that aider sends with `--verbose`. By default aider selects the most useful subset of the map which will fit into 1024 tokens. You can allow it to use more tokens with `--map-tokens`.

The best way to use aider right now is to tell it which files need to be edited if you know (per the [tips](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider#tips)). Aider will use the repo map to help make sure GPT understands how that code fits into the larger repo.

body:
So I have this implemented in a branch. But I actually don't even bother asking the user to make a decision. If GPT tries to edit a dirty file, aider will just commit the dirty changes (with a nice message) before applying and committing GPT's edits.

This seems sensible, low friction and less confusing. You now never get interrupted and asked about pending dirty changes. Aider just commits them for you to keep them distinct from GPT's edits and preserve the ability to cleanly undo GPT's changes. And dirty changes are only ever committed by aider if the file is about to get modified by GPT.

As always, aider still respects the `--no-dirty-commits` flag. If set, it will apply GPT's edits without first committing dirty files.

body:
Thanks for trying aider!

Which models are you wanting to switch from and to?

In some cases, it would be very hard to change the model mid-conversation. Changing from gpt-4 to gpt-3.5 or vice-versa would also require changing the "edit format" and rewriting all of the conversation history. Changing between different versions of 3.5 or between different versions of 4 might be possible.

But in practice I'm not sure how useful this feature would be? gpt-3.5-16k is pretty inexpensive, so why not just use it always? And for gpt-4, very few people have access to gpt-4-32k, so almost no one would have the ability to increase the context window size mid-conversation.

author: joshuavial

body:
(copying this comment from discord)

It seems like a nice to have feature.

The real work is looking at each cmd line switch and deciding which bin it falls into:

1. Trivial to dynamically change at runtime. Something like `--verbose` or `--map-tokens`.

2. Possible to dynamically change at runtime, with special extra work when it changes. Something like `--model` could be made dynamic, as long as you only switch between identical models with different context windows. Or if you always discard the conversation history when you switch model (but is this really dynamic then). Other switches could have similar special limitations or requirements.

3. Impossible to sensibly make dynamic, like `--openai-api-base`.

After we do that binning, is it still worth adding a `/set` command? Or are there too few useful switches that we're willing to do the work to support? Or are we making a big complex machine to support the more complex switches (like `--model`) which will slow down and complicate future innovative work?

You can now specify a float for the `use_temperature` model setting, like this:

```yaml
- name: fireworks_ai/accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-r1
  edit_format: diff
  weak_model_name: fireworks_ai/accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v3
  use_repo_map: true
  use_temperature: false
  streaming: true
  editor_model_name: fireworks_ai/accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v3
  editor_edit_format: editor-diff
  remove_reasoning: think
  extra_params:
      max_tokens: 160000
  use_temperature: 0.5
```

aider --install-main-branch

body:
For future reference, I don't believe that downgrading your index version is supported. I ended up deleting my index (while the repo was fully checked in and backed up) and running git reset.

Digging into it a little deeper, the issue is because GitPython only supports index version 1 and 2 ([relevant code](https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/blob/main/git/index/fun.py#L210)), and since the project is in [maintenance mode](https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/tree/main?tab=readme-ov-file#development-status) it seems like there is a decent change that this won't be fixed in near future (though the GitPython maintainer is open to merging feature contributions).

Hopefully the authors successor project [GitOxide](https://github.com/Byron/gitoxide) will be stable and have a Python binding at some point soon.

body:
Since this was new to me and the official documentation about git index versions is quite dense, I asked Sonnet-3.5 and ChatGPT for clarification, with ChatGPT producing a much better answer in this case (may be helpful for others, hopefully):

--- AI slop start ---

Git index versions (2, 3, and 4) represent different formats of the index file (also known as the staging area) that Git uses to track the state of your working directory between commits. Here's an explanation of the key points regarding when the index version changes, the default version, and how certain Git features might force an index upgrade.

### 1. **Default Git Index Version**
   - **Version 2** is the **default** index version used by Git. This is the version that most tools, like GitPython, typically interact with.
   - **Version 3** and **Version 4** were introduced to support new features, but Git only upgrades the index version when certain features are used that require these newer formats.

### 2. **Index Upgrades via Git Features**
   Git will upgrade the index version under specific circumstances, often related to optimizations or special features that require newer formats.

   - **Version 3** introduced:
     - Path compression in the index (optimized storage for file paths).
     - Version 3 is not widely used, and its adoption has been limited.
   
   - **Version 4** introduced:
     - **Cache tree extensions**: These are optimizations for handling large repositories, particularly with submodules or large numbers of files.
     - **Support for SHA-256 hash algorithm**: This could be relevant for future cryptographic algorithm changes.
     - **Sparse index**: For large repositories, this feature makes Git operations faster by only loading part of the working directory's index into memory.
   
   Git does not automatically upgrade the index unless you explicitly use features that require a newer version. For example, working with very large repositories or using experimental features (like the SHA-256 transition) may force an upgrade to version 4.

### 3. **How Git Index Version Is Set**
   - You can set the index version manually by running:
     ```bash
     git update-index --index-version=<2|3|4>
     ```
   - **However**, Git will automatically upgrade the index if you use features that require a higher version, as mentioned above.

### 4. **Ensuring Compatibility with GitPython**
   Since GitPython only supports **version 2**, the safest approach is to:
   - Avoid features that require newer index versions (particularly in large repositories with features like cache tree extensions).
   - Regularly check the index version with:
     ```bash
     git ls-files --debug | grep index
     ```
   - If needed, you can manually downgrade the index version back to version 2 using the following command:
     ```bash
     git update-index --index-version=2
     ```

### Conclusion
If you're using basic Git features (commits, branches, diffs, etc.), the index will likely stay at version 2. However, advanced features like sparse checkouts, experimental SHA-256 support, or very large repositories may trigger an automatic upgrade to version 4. As long as you avoid these scenarios, the repository should remain compatible with tools that use GitPython.

--- AI slop end ---

body:
while there isn't support for XDG, an alternative to symlinking files is to configure an alias:

```sh
# e.g. in ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, etc. or some script that those scripts source

# aider
if type "aider" >/dev/null; then
  alias aider='aider \
    --chat-history-file ~/.config/aider/.aider.chat.history.md \
    --input-history-file ~/.config/aider/.aider.input.history \
    --config ~/.config/aider/.aider.conf.yml \
    --env-file ~/.config/aider/.env
  '
fi
```

Which assumes you're using the following directory structure:

```shell
.config
├── aider
│   ├── .aider.conf.yml
│   └── .env
```

This alias starts aider without any specified models, so to pass additional parameters you can use `--`:

```sh
$  aider -- --architect \
    --model openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-r1 \
    --editor-model openrouter/anthropic/claude-3.7-sonnet \
    --watch-files
```

A justfile can make it simpler to configure various preferred starting parameters

EDIT: here are my dotfiles for context: https://github.com/larrybotha/dotfiles/commit/fd69ad2917aa0675e60330f61688ca14a5425b7d

body:
Hello all,

I've also been enjoying using Aider, and have a few tricks to solve similar situations:

1. You can change the description of your current git commit with `git commit --amend`. This is a good idea to do before you do deep explorations so you can see and revert to a known good git. You can also do `git commit --amend -m "<commit message>"` if you wish to do it in one line.
2. I often will work with two or more branches, one that is `spike`, where experiments are going that may or may not succeed, as well as `dev` where changes that will eventually go into a merge/pull request live. If the `spike` turns out not to be what I want or need, I can just reset / force it back to `dev`.

body:
I'm sorry, I don't think I described the functionality well.  The idea is not to run a test once, but to run the test after every change, and to re-submit any prompt that causes a test to fail, in a loop until you get test success (or a max retries).  Example scenario:

1. `/test-command npm run test`
2. `/test-first on`  - The changes the system prompt to instruct GPT-4 to work in a TDD manner, by generating tests first, when possible.
3. Prompt: "create a library function in util/lib.ts to do a quicksort"  -  This results in the generation of a unit test and the implementation code, as instructed in the system prompt.
4. Test runs and fails.  Implementation (but not the test) is re-generated.
6. Test runs and fails.  Implementation is re-generated.
8. Test runs and fails.  Implementation is re-generated.   (this could go on for 7 more times)
10. Test runs and succeeds.

I know this may seem out of scope of your simple project, but it would greatly increase success rate of codegen prompts.

body:
One way to do it is to teach the LLM that it is allowed to write TODO comments, or for some languages like Kotlin, you can call a `TODO("implement me")` function (it throws at runtime).

This would allow the LLM to defer work if it's not sure it can do it all at once. Then if you detect it emitted such a function call, you go back and ask it to fix that specific TODO, but you can potentially do them in parallel if the expression is being used inside typed functions.

body:
Hi @achristianson @paul-gauthier LiteLLM now allows you to queue requests. It's built to solve the problem in this issue (would love your feedback if not)

Here's a quick start on using it: Compatible with GPT-4, llama (mentioned in this thread) 
docs: https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/routing#queuing-beta 

### Quick Start 

1. Add Redis credentials in a .env file

```python
REDIS_HOST="my-redis-endpoint"
REDIS_PORT="my-redis-port"
REDIS_PASSWORD="my-redis-password" # [OPTIONAL] if self-hosted
REDIS_USERNAME="default" # [OPTIONAL] if self-hosted
```

2. Start litellm server with your model config

```bash
$ litellm --config /path/to/config.yaml --use_queue
```

Here's an example config for `gpt-3.5-turbo`

**config.yaml** (This will load balance between OpenAI + Azure endpoints)
```yaml
model_list: 
  - model_name: gpt-3.5-turbo
    litellm_params: 
      model: gpt-3.5-turbo
      api_key: 
  - model_name: gpt-3.5-turbo
    litellm_params: 
      model: azure/chatgpt-v-2 # actual model name
      api_key: 
      api_version: 2023-07-01-preview
      api_base: https://openai-gpt-4-test-v-1.openai.azure.com/
```

3. Test (in another window) → sends 100 simultaneous requests to the queue 

```bash
$ litellm --test_async --num_requests 100
```


### Available Endpoints
- `/queue/request` - Queues a /chat/completions request. Returns a job id. 
- `/queue/response/{id}` - Returns the status of a job. If completed, returns the response as well. Potential status's are: `queued` and `finished`.

Are you talking about behaviour using gpt-3.5 or gpt-4 as they use quite different formats for their output

I've been frustrated with large diffs from gpt-4 a lot - mostly from the extra time it takes before getting to code I can review. My work around has been to add a "please create a minimal diff" which makes it smaller, but also more fragile. I recall seeing a comment in discord or a previous issue along the lines of "the more code in the wrapping diff, the higher the quality of the new code written" but I haven't dug into it much.

I've also found that writing small files, small functions and giving aider small changes (practices I like anyway) becomes more important when working with aider - as well as having good test coverage etc.

I have wondered about a "custom instructions" sort of feature where a user could include some instructions in the config (so could be applied on a per project, or global level) which might be a more general way to have impact on this issue.

Yep, I was talking about gpt-4.

One solution I was imagining was to take advantage of the c-tags. Maybe aider could output the location that he wants to replace, instead of writing out the head of the diff. It could output a custom format like:

```python
\```python
<<<<<<<< HEAD
#diff[20,25]
========
...content...
>>>>>>>> this
\```
```

which would replace lines 20 through 25 with the new content. This could be rendered in the terminal as an actual diff all at once, instead of one token at a time.
author: samhaaf

body:
"the more code in the wrapping diff, the higher the quality of the new code written"

To that end, aider could split the output generation into two completions. 

First completion: would do logical reasoning and select the location of the diff

Locally: #diff[l,k] gets replaced with the content from the file, and some surrounding lines for context. Maybe each line is given a line number, for clarity.

Second completion: is given the updated response of the first completion and asked to complete the output. 

Downsides:
- Twice as many requests with the same full context, so more API costs (doesn't bother me)
- ctags don't store the end of a function definition, only the beginning. It might require custom code to read the files and find the end of the function definition. But maybe somebody else put out a repo for this. 
- Might be difficult to constrain gpt-4 to write an incomplete response. I have a tough time constraining it to do much simpler things. It tends to ignore instructions in the presence of complex problems.
author: samhaaf

body:
Thanks for the suggestion. I've tried many variations of the approaches you are describing. 

The results are very consistently worse when you try and optimize in these ways. Trying to have GPT use line numbers or be very terse in the diffs that it's generating harms its ability to write good code. 

For a longer discussion of this, see the linked blog post below.

https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html
author: paul-gauthier

body: It's worth noting that how hard you get hit by this depends on the language. In something like Kotlin it's very easy to pull code out into separate files or functions using the IDE, and that doesn't require updating imports when it's in the same package, so keeping files small and top level definitions minimal is quite easy. In Python it's not quite so easy, but I wonder if the better path isn't to slightly alter how scripting languages load code, rather than try to beat GPT into being more concise.

A large portion of the prompt text in `coders/xxx_prompts.py` is very closely tied to the specifics of the python coder implementation in the matched file `coders/xxx_coder.py`. author: mikehearn

body:
The purpose of the `.gitignore` file is to make sure git doesn't consider *new* files that match when doing `git status` and refuses to add them with `git add`.

Files that match which are *already* in the repo are still part of the repo. So it would be odd for aider to use `.gitignore` to additionally mean "but ignore them for aider purposes". That's what `.aiderignore` is for.

author: paul-gauthier

body:
I would expect much better results with a grammar that constrains the llm to selecting a tool, and populating appropriate fields for that tool with appropriate values (rather than ANY freeform output except in text fields), with quite surgical tools + tests / lints.

I'm toying with the idea of writing something similar to aider with strict constrained grammars and pydantic-based typing/tools plugins to test this, but would be happy to not have to :)

If you have any preliminary results from something like that, I'd be interested.  Certainly very interested if you produce benchmarks similar to the article but with constraints.

Do agree that newer models should be (somewhat) better at this, either way.  It's probably related to model size too.

# global

body:
> I actually think this is probably reasonable behavior. It's not clear that you want aider to pull in the (potentially very large amount of) code from submodules. But I'm open to input on this if you have a specific need.

Having the submodules indexed in the repomap would actually be really helpful when dealing with dependencies that are either not public or not widely used, so the LLM in use is likely not aware of which specific APIs exist, what their signatures are, and what their semantics are (the result of this is that the LLM is almost guaranteed to allucinate these APIs it does not know anything about).

This is probably also true of any dependency (regardless of it being a submodule, a vendored subdirectory, or just a reference in a requirements.txt, go.mod, pom.xml, or anything else).

The size of the repomap is definitely going to be a concern, but it's effectively the [same problem as having a large codebase](https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html#optimizing-the-map)... so maybe this could be improved by teaching aider to pull in additional parts of the repomap on demand.

@paul-gauthier if you think it's warranted, I can file a new issue to reconsider this.

body:
Generally speaking, it's a bad idea to do `git add .` as it will literally add every file in every subdirectory to your git repository. That's usually not what you want, as there are often config, cache, virtual environments, installed packages, etc that will get put into git that way.

That said, it appears that yarn actually encourages people to commit parts of the the `.yarn` subdir to git. Which is an unexpected stance to take.

If you didn't mean/want to have `.yarn` in git, you could do something like the below commands. But it's your repo, so you should understand the commands below and their potential dangers and implications before running them.

```
git rm -r --cached .yarn
echo .yarn >> .gitignore
```

Also, the errors like these are harmless. Aider is just warning you that it can't read the file as text. These warning messages are annoying, but nothing bad is happening.

```
C:\code\devops\ai-consumer-chatbot\.yarn\cache\@discoveryjs-json-ext-npm-0.5.7-fe04af1f31-2176d301cc.zip: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xae in position 11: invalid start byte
Use --encoding to set the unicode encoding.

I think the key topic here is how to effectively navigate code bases with millions of lines of code. AIs are pretty similar to humans. They can only hold so much personal knowledge of the code to aid them with navigating it. 

Much of the navigation of code is through experiences. If you are having a problem with X, you might also need to access Y and Z. This is memory. And this comes from real world experiences and history. 

In large code bases ( ie millions of LOC ) the only way I can see this working is to have a team of specialists. Each with their memories of the code. And each focusing on certain areas. Then have that Team try to solve the problem. 

In effect, autogen with aider as an example.
